cinema-002.title: A tall recording inside a wide frame
cinema-002.alt: A tall, narrow photograph sits in the middle of a wide black rectangle, with black bars filling the space on both sides. It shows a gravel track beside a grass verge, a stack of logs and trees under a blue sky.
cinema-002.caption: Look at the black bars. This picture was recorded tall and is being shown in a wide frame, so the bars take up about two thirds of the width and the image cannot grow to use them. The shape is fixed at the moment of recording. That is why this lesson has you choose it first and then fit the whole movement inside it.

cinema-003.title: A wider view answers what is happening
cinema-003.alt: A black and white film still. A man in a light shirt stands on a flat rail wagon and leans one elbow on the muzzle of a large mortar, resting his head on his hand. Cannonballs are stacked at his feet, and a fence and a field lie behind.
cinema-003.caption: This still from The General, a 1926 film, shows the whole man, the mortar and the wagon they stand on. At this size you can read the situation: he is leaning on the gun with his head resting on his hand, beside a pile of cannonballs. You cannot read much of his face, and the picture does not need you to. The next still comes from another moment in the same film.

credit.work: The General (1926 film), still with the mortar
credit.author: Buster Keaton

cinema-003.title: A closer view makes the face readable
cinema-003.alt: A black and white film still. A man with wide eyes leans forward over the front of a steam locomotive, gripping its lowest bar with both hands. His face is near the middle of the picture.
cinema-003.caption: Now the camera is close enough to make one thing readable: his face. The wide eyes and the grip on the bar are the information, and the locomotive shrinks to a background. Both stills are sharp and well lit. They differ in the fact each one makes readable, which is how this lesson asks you to choose a shot size.

credit.work: The General (1926 film), still on the locomotive
credit.author: Buster Keaton

cinema-004.title: A thirds grid on a real photograph
cinema-004.alt: A road runs from the bottom edge of the picture toward a bright, misty opening in a dark forest. Red lines divide the picture into thirds each way, and the opening lies close to where the upper and right lines cross.
cinema-004.caption: Look at the bright opening first. It lies close to the point where two grid lines cross, and the road runs up from the bottom edge to meet it. The grid did not make the picture work. The road gives the bright space a job, as the route into it, which is the test this lesson asks you to apply. The red lines were drawn on afterwards to demonstrate the idea.

cinema-007.title: Clipped highlights, marked in red
cinema-007.alt: Two copies of one photograph, stacked. A man leans in beside a heavy metal press while an older man in a pale jacket and a younger man stand behind him. In the lower copy the brightest areas are painted red: the bright background at the upper left, parts of the pale jacket and a patch of the metal table.
cinema-007.caption: Compare the two copies. The upper one is the photograph as recorded. In the lower one every pixel that reached pure white has been painted red. Those red patches hold no detail at all, so no slider can bring the folds of the pale jacket or the surface of the table back. This is a different scene from the towel, and the same kind of loss.

cinema-008.title: What a very close camera does to sizes
cinema-008.alt: A dog's face photographed from very close with a wide lens. The nose fills the middle of the picture and looks far larger than the eyes and ears behind it.
cinema-008.caption: Look at the nose, then the eyes and ears. The camera was very close to the nose, so the eyes and ears were much farther from the lens than the nose was, and they are drawn much smaller. Enlarging a picture taken from across the room would grow the nose and ears together and keep their real proportions. It is the two paper houses again, with a much bigger distance ratio.

credit.work: Dog pictured from very close with a 0.5x lens
credit.author: Jsw618

cinema-009.title: A low camera changes what rises above what
cinema-009.alt: A bronze monument photographed from near the ground: a group of figures, one of them pointing, with a flag raised above them. It towers against a blue sky beside a brick church spire.
cinema-009.caption: Look at what this low camera can and cannot see. It is close to the monument and far below it, so the top of the flag reaches almost as high in the picture as the church spire. The top of the stone base is hidden. Lift the camera and that surface would come into view, as the inside of the box does in this lesson. Describe that visible change first. Calling a low view powerful is a reading added afterwards. The monument stands in Overmere, Belgium.

credit.work: Low-angle shot of Onze-Lieve-Vrouw-Hemelvaartkerk and Boerenkrijgmonument, Overmere, 2026
credit.author: DimiTalen

cinema-010.title: Depth from overlap, with nothing blurred
cinema-010.alt: Dark trees stand in the foreground. Behind them a valley lies in haze, and a faint mountain rises beyond it under a bright, hazy sky.
cinema-010.caption: Count the layers. Dark trees overlap a hazy valley, and beyond the valley a faint mountain stands against the sky. Near, middle and far are easy to tell apart without any background blur, because each layer covers part of the next and has its own tone. This view over the Kathmandu Valley gets its separation from haze. Your tabletop gets it from where you put the camera.

credit.work: Kathmandu Valley and hillside pine trees from Shivapuri
credit.author: Krishna k. sahh

cinema-011.title: The same keys, shaken and steadied
cinema-011.alt: Two photographs of the same calculator keypad. In the upper one, labeled IS Off, the numbers are smeared. In the lower one, labeled IS On, the numbers are crisp.
cinema-011.caption: Compare the number 5 in each half. Both pictures show the same keys at the same size. In the upper one the camera moved while the picture was being recorded, so every edge is smeared. In the lower one the optical image stabilizer, the IS in the labels, was switched on and countered that movement. Resting your arms on something solid attacks the same problem earlier, before any shake reaches the camera.

cinema-012.title: One picture that gathered light during a pan
cinema-012.alt: A dark blue-green racing car with an orange nose, number 2, is sharp, while the grass and track around it are smeared into horizontal streaks. The driver wears a white helmet.
cinema-012.caption: Look at the streaks behind the car. The photographer swung the camera with the car while this single picture was gathering light. The car stayed in one place in the frame, so it is sharp. The grass crossed the frame during that time, so it smeared. The length of that smear depends on how long each picture gathers light. How many pictures are taken each second is a separate setting.

cinema-014.title: Blocking on a stage
cinema-014.alt: A theater stage seen from the audience. At the center a man in gray and a woman in a red dress face each other, with a hand raised to a face between them. Seven other actors stand spread out to the left and right, none of them in front of the pair.
cinema-014.caption: Find the pair at the center, then check who stands in front of them: nobody. A theater audience cannot move, so where the actors stand decides what it can see. Here the central exchange is open to every seat and the other actors stand to the sides. Your lens is that audience. This is a university production of Macbeth. Arranging the people before any camera decision is what film crews also call blocking.

cinema-015.title: One side of the line, and what crossing does
cinema-015.alt: A diagram seen from above. Two people face each other in the middle of a circle, and a dashed line through them divides the circle into a green half and a pink half. Cameras stand along the green arc and one camera stands in the pink half. Two small frames above show the pair from each half, with the two people on opposite sides of the screen in each.
cinema-015.caption: Find the dashed line through the two people. That is the line of this lesson, the net across the tennis court. Follow the thin arrow up from the cameras on the green side to their frame: orange on the left of the screen, blue on the right. Now follow the arrow up from the single camera on the pink side. In its frame the two have swapped places. Each frame is fine alone. The broken red arrow between them marks the cut that would confuse a viewer, because the room would seem to flip.

credit.author: Grm wnr
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

cinema-016.title: A slate ties each recording to the list
cinema-016.alt: A hand holds up a film slate with its clapper arm raised. Its top boxes read 2, 1 and 12, above a red timecode display and the handwritten title Follow Me.
cinema-016.caption: Read the numbers along the top. The first box is the roll, 2, and the last is the take, 12. The number between them identifies the shot. A crew films this board at the start of every recording, so that each clip can be matched to its line in the shot list later. The board says which shot this is. Only the list says what the shot is for, and that is the entry this lesson asks you to write.

cinema-017.title: Several cameras share one moment
cinema-017.alt: A large television news studio seen from a balcony. One presenter sits at a round desk in the middle. About five studio cameras on wheeled stands face the desk, and staff sit at monitors in the foreground.
cinema-017.caption: Count the cameras pointed toward the one presenter. Running together, they record the same moment, so any two of their views show the same stage of every gesture, and a cut between them always has somewhere to land. With one phone you build that overlap yourself: perform the whole movement again, start to finish, for each view. This is the Al Jazeera English news studio in Doha.

cinema-018.title: Continuity has long been a job on set
cinema-018.alt: A black and white photograph on a film set. A woman in uniform writes on a large board resting on her lap, seated beside a man in uniform who leans forward watching. Two soldiers sit behind them, and dark film equipment stands at the upper left.
cinema-018.caption: Look at what she is doing while the director watches: writing. Her job on this wartime set at Pinewood Studios in England was continuity, a written record of how props, clothes and positions stood in each take, so that the next take could start from the same state. Your reset record is the same idea, cut down to the few details a viewer actually follows.

credit.work: Film and Photography during the Second World War H21451
credit.author: War Office official photographer, Malindine E G (Lt), Puttnam L (Lt)

cinema-019.title: Direction happens in conversation
cinema-019.alt: A black and white photograph of three people standing close together and smiling: a woman in a polka dot blouse raising one finger, a man in a dark suit with clasped hands, and an older man in a hat and a tweed suit.
cinema-019.caption: This was taken during the filming of When Tomorrow Comes in 1939. The actors Irene Dunne and Charles Boyer are talking with the director, John M. Stahl. A photograph cannot tell you what was said. It does show where direction happens: in a conversation before the camera runs, where a performer can be handed something to try and can answer back.

credit.work: Backstage photograph on the set of When Tomorrow Comes
credit.author: Unknown author

cinema-024.title: A harbor small enough to wade through
cinema-024.alt: A black and white photograph of a model harbor built in shallow water. One man stands on a small raft holding a long pole and others stand in the water among model warships. Model docks and buildings line the shore behind.
cinema-024.caption: Use the men for scale. They are standing in a model of Pearl Harbor built in Japan for a 1942 film about the attack. A Japanese studio could not film the real harbor. On screen the ships and the shoreline kept their positions relative to each other, and that relationship was all the audience needed. Your paper train on a table is the same decision at a smaller size.

cinema-025.title: Window light in Vermeer's The Milkmaid
cinema-025.alt: A painting of a woman in a yellow bodice and blue apron pouring milk at a table. Daylight enters by a window at the upper left and lights her forehead, her forearms and the bread.
cinema-025.caption: Find the window at the upper left, then follow its light. It reaches her forehead, her near forearm and the bread first, and the side of her face turned from the window falls into shade. Vermeer painted this around 1660, long before cameras, and faced your problem: the window stays where it is, so the choice left is where to stand.

cinema-026.title: Why a shadow has a soft edge at all
cinema-026.alt: A diagram of the Sun, the Earth and the Earth's shadow. A dark cone behind the Earth is labeled Umbra. A paler region around it is labeled Penumbra. Small inset pictures show the Sun fully hidden, partly hidden, and showing as a ring.
cinema-026.caption: Find the dark core behind the Earth, then the paler band around it. In the core the Earth hides the whole Sun. In the band it hides only part of the Sun, so some light still arrives. That band is the gradual edge this lesson has you judge. A wide light source makes the band wide, and a small one leaves almost none. Astronomers call the core the umbra and the band the penumbra.

cinema-027.title: The same trick with a bigger sheet
cinema-027.alt: A photo shoot on a rocky shore with bright surf behind. A young woman in light, sleeveless summer clothes stands by dark rocks on the left. Beside her a person in a dark jacket holds up a large round reflector, and a photographer crouches on the right.
cinema-027.caption: Find the large round disc held up beside the model. It is a folding reflector, positioned to bounce sunlight onto her. Notice how dark the two crew members look against the bright surf, while the model beside the disc is easy to see. The disc does the job of your sheet of paper, at a larger size.

cinema-029.title: A light source you can place without seeing it
cinema-029.alt: A painting of two women and a swaddled newborn in darkness. The woman on the left raises one hand, which hides a candle. Its light falls on the baby held by the woman on the right and on both women's faces.
cinema-029.caption: Find the light source before you read on. It is a candle, hidden behind the raised hand of the woman on the left. You cannot see the flame, yet you can tell where it is: the baby and both faces are bright on the sides turned toward that hand and dark on the sides turned away. Georges de La Tour painted this in the 1640s. A lamp in your shot explains the light only when the page sits where that light really lands.

cinema-030.title: Bright steps behind, no faces in front
cinema-030.alt: Three stone arches seen from inside a dark arcade. Through them, sunlit steps rise in bright light. Three people, one taller and two smaller, stand inside the arcade in front of the arches as black shapes with no visible features.
cinema-030.caption: Look at the three people standing in front of the arches. The sunlit steps behind them are far brighter than the shade they stand in. The brightness of this picture suits the steps, so the people became black shapes with no faces. It is the bright doorway behind your head, at the size of a building. The fix in this lesson applies here too: bring light onto the face, or change what sits behind it. This is the arcade below Bethesda Terrace in Central Park, New York.

credit.work: Below Bethesda Terrace in the Central Park
credit.author: Jorge Quinteros from Brooklyn, USA

cinema-031.title: Three lamps, one camera setting
cinema-031.alt: Three lit lamps in one fitting. The one at the upper left glows warm yellow and is labeled about 2700 K, 60 W incandescent. The one on the right is a paler warm white, labeled 3500 K, 13 W fluorescent. The one at the bottom is the whitest, labeled 5500 K, 13 W fluorescent.
cinema-031.caption: Three lamps share one fitting, and one camera setting recorded all three. The lamp at the upper left looks warm yellow, the one on the right a paler warm white, and the one at the bottom the whitest of the three. The camera could treat only one of them as white. The numbers are color temperatures in kelvin, and a lower number means a warmer, more orange light. Your window and your desk lamp differ in the same way.

cinema-032.title: Bands that exist only in the recording
cinema-032.alt: A close view of a glowing lamp against black. Narrow light and dark stripes run across the whole lit surface.
cinema-032.caption: Look at the stripes across this lamp. They are not on the lamp. It is an LED bulb dimmed to its lowest setting, and its light is pulsing faster than the eye can follow. A phone camera records a picture line by line, each a moment after the last, so some lines caught the lamp brighter and others caught it dimmer. The same disagreement in timing is what puts moving bands across your instruction card.

credit.work: Flickering LED lamp visible via rolling shutter
credit.author: Ragesoss

cinema-035.title: Twelve attempts on one sheet
cinema-035.alt: A sheet of twelve small black and white photographs in three rows. Each shows the same woman in a dress with a full skirt, hands on her hips, posing by water with the Washington Monument behind her. Some frames show her full length and others closer.
cinema-035.caption: Twelve attempts at one picture, printed together on a single sheet. The photographer Toni Frissell made them around 1946 for a fashion advertisement, with the Washington Monument behind the model. Compare the frames: the pose and the model's position against the monument change from one to the next. A sheet like this exists so that one frame can be chosen for what it contains. Your three recordings of the coat pocket are the same kind of sheet.

credit.work: Toni Frissell, fashion model near tidal basin, Washington, D.C., ca. 1946
credit.author: Toni Frissell

cinema-036.title: When every join was a real cut
cinema-036.alt: A man in a brown sweater sits at a large blue-gray flatbed film editing table. Reels of film lie flat on round plates, and a small tilted screen sits at the back of the table. A black lamp on an arm and a wooden rack of hanging film strips stand by the wall behind the table, and a gray telephone sits in the foreground.
cinema-036.caption: This is a flatbed editing table. Film runs across it from one plate to another, past a small screen, and the editor cuts the strip and joins it by hand. Fades and dissolves could not be made here. They were made later at a laboratory, so editors first got the order right with plain cuts and watched the result. Editing apps make effects instant, but that order of work still holds.

cinema-037.title: One stride, cut into stages
cinema-037.alt: A printed card of twelve small photographs in three rows, titled The Horse in Motion. Eleven show a horse and rider in silhouette at successive moments of a gallop. The twelfth shows the horse standing still.
cinema-037.caption: Read the pictures in order, left to right and row by row. The first eleven show one gallop, each a little further on than the one before, and the twelfth shows the horse standing. Now suppose you cut to another camera in the middle of this run. The first picture of the new view has to show the stride at the stage where the old view left it, or the horse seems to jump back. Eadweard Muybridge took these in California in 1878.

cinema-039.title: A card that had to be read to work
cinema-039.alt: A black and white cinema card in a decorative frame. A woman in a very large feathered hat faces the viewer while a man and a woman peer around it from behind her, with more faces in the dark behind them. The lettering reads: Madam, how would you like to sit behind the hat you are wearing.
cinema-039.caption: Read the card, and notice how long it takes you. Cards like this were shown on cinema screens around 1912. Everything it has to say is in the lettering, so it was worth nothing unless it stayed up long enough to be read to the last word. Your doorstep note works the same way: the clock for the viewer's response starts when the words can be read, not when the card first appears.

cinema-043.title: A reference that is the same in every shot
cinema-043.alt: Two hands hold a card of 24 colored squares in front of a checked shirt. The bottom row of squares runs from white through grays to black.
cinema-043.caption: This card is a color reference. Its 24 squares have known colors, and the bottom row runs from white through grays to black. Film crews record a card like it for a moment in each setup. Later, two shots can be matched by making the same squares look the same in both. Your white page does that job with a single patch, and it costs nothing.

cinema-045.title: A crew pays for closeness
cinema-045.alt: A small film crew on the deck of a boat beside a stone bridge. One man carries a large camera on a body harness. A second man in headphones holds a long pole level, and the gray, furry microphone at its end hangs toward a seated man in a blue jacket.
cinema-045.caption: Follow the pole from the man in headphones to its furry gray tip. That tip is a microphone, and he is holding it out over the deck toward the seated man who is being filmed. Crews go to this trouble for the reason in this lesson: the nearer a microphone is to the mouth, the more voice it records compared with the room, the water and the traffic. This crew is filming on a boat on the Seine in Paris.

cinema-048.title: A room built for replacing a voice
cinema-048.alt: A man sits at a mixing desk with two screens, one showing an audio timeline and one showing a cartoon. A window above the desk looks into a recording booth that has its own screen showing the same cartoon.
cinema-048.caption: A dubbing studio. Through the window is the recording booth, with its own screen, where a performer watches the picture while speaking the line. At the desk, an engineer plays the same picture and records each attempt. The whole room is built around one problem from this lesson: a new voice has to land on the starts, pauses and endings of a picture that already exists.

cinema-049.title: A sound effect being performed
cinema-049.alt: A black and white photograph. A man in a hat and waistcoat saws a plank on a wooden crate with a bow saw. Beside him a man in a white coat holds a microphone toward the saw.
cinema-049.caption: One man saws a plank while another holds a microphone toward the cut. They are recording a sound effect for Finnish radio, probably in the 1930s. Look at what is controlled: the action is performed on purpose, the microphone is pointed at the contact that makes the sound, and the take can be repeated until it is right. Your shoe on two surfaces is the same method with a quieter prop.

credit.work: A man is recording sound effects, 1930s
credit.author: Archives of the Finnish Broadcasting Company Yle

cinema-051.title: Two names on one disc
cinema-051.alt: A close view of an early flat gramophone disc. Lettering stamped into it reads E. Berliner's Gramophone, Blue Bells of Scotland, Trombone Solo by Mr. Arthur Pryor, with a date in August 1897.
cinema-051.caption: Read the lettering stamped into this disc. One line names the tune, Blue Bells of Scotland. Another names the player and carries a date: a trombone solo by Mr. Arthur Pryor, August 1897. Those are two different things. Someone wrote the tune. This disc holds one performance of it, by one player, on one day. A soundtrack note has to check both, even when the title on your screen shows only one.

credit.work: Blue Bells of Scotland, trombone solo
credit.author: Arthur Pryor, Berliner Gramophone Co.

cinema-052.title: What a clipped peak looks like
cinema-052.alt: The screen of an oscilloscope showing a bright wave. The wave rises and falls smoothly, but each top and each bottom is cut off flat.
cinema-052.caption: The line on this screen should be a smooth wave with rounded tops and bottoms. Look at the flat ends instead. The equipment could go no higher and no lower, so it cut the wave off there, and the shape that belonged beyond the flat part is gone. This is clipping, and you hear it as harsh distortion. Notice what it cannot tell you: a signal can avoid clipping while the words in it are still buried under another sound.

cinema-059.title: A working storyboard is rough
cinema-059.alt: A storyboard page with six boxes. Each holds a quick sketch of cartoon characters in blue line, with a handwritten scene number and background note above it and typed lines of dialogue below it.
cinema-059.caption: Look at how rough these panels are. Each one is a quick sketch in blue line, with a scene number, a note about the background, and the dialogue typed underneath. Nobody would frame it, and it does its job: anyone can see who is on screen, how large, and what is said. Tom Ray drew this page for an episode of The Radio Adventures of Dr. Floyd. Your scarf and tote need even less drawing.

credit.work: Storyboard for The Radio Adventures of Dr. Floyd
credit.author: Tom Ray

design-002.title: Three directions a color can move
design-002.alt: A diagram titled Munsell Color System. A vertical column of grays runs from black at 0 to white at 10. A ring of ten named hues surrounds its middle, from red through yellow, green and blue to purple. One purple-blue arm reaches outward from the column, numbered from 0 to 12. A small key at the upper left names the three directions: value, hue and chroma.
design-002.caption: This diagram gives every color three addresses. Going around the ring changes the hue: red, yellow, green, blue, purple. Going up the middle column changes the value, from black at 0 to white at 10. Going outward along the purple-blue arm makes the color stronger, from gray at the column to vivid at the tip. This system calls that chroma, and this lesson calls it saturation. Darkening your basil green is a move down the column. Muting it is a move inward toward the gray. Those are different directions.

credit.author: Jacob Rus
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

design-003.title: One gray that looks like a fade
design-003.alt: A horizontal gray bar lies across a background that fades from black on the left to white on the right. The bar looks lighter at its left end and darker at its right end.
design-003.caption: Look along the gray bar from left to right. It seems to fade from a light gray to a darker one. It does not. The bar is one flat gray along its whole length, and only the background changes, from black to white. Cover the background above and below the bar with two strips of paper and the fade disappears. Your drawing between two mounts is this bar: the sample stays the same and the surround does the changing.

design-004.title: Every blue beside an amber window
design-004.alt: A snow-covered old town in dim light. The sky, the hills and the snow are all shades of blue, and small windows and one stone tower glow amber.
design-004.caption: Start with the lit windows and the glowing tower. Beside that amber, every blue in this picture looks cool. Now hide the windows with a finger and compare the blue of the sky with the blue of the snow. Is one of them warmer than the other? You can only answer by naming both, which is how this lesson asks you to use the words. This is the old town of Zug in Switzerland at blue hour, the short time when the sun is just below the horizon.

credit.work: CH.ZG.Zug View from Guggi 01 16x9+R 8192x4608 Br058 gp denoising Br075
credit.author: Roy Egloff

design-005.title: Is the red an accent here?
design-005.alt: A poster with a gray-blue panel between cream margins. The word PET is brushed in red at the top. Below it are the heads of two dogs in black line with white patches, and the word SHOW in yellow outline slants across the lower half. Small lettering at the bottom reads WPA Recreation Project, Dist. No. 2.
design-005.caption: Count the colors on this poster from the late 1930s: a gray-blue panel on cream, black and white for the two dogs, red for one word and yellow for the other. Now run this lesson's check and cover the red with a finger. The word PET is gone, and only the two dogs still hint at what kind of show this is. So the red is not an accent here. It carries information, and the design depends on it. The poster was printed by silkscreen, a process that lays down one flat color at a time.

credit.work: Pet show, WPA recreation project poster (1936 to 1939)
credit.author: Work Projects Administration Poster Collection

design-006.title: Red, green and blue light on one wall
design-006.alt: Three overlapping pools of colored light on a brick wall in a dark room: green at the upper left, blue at the upper right and red at the bottom. Where two pools overlap the wall looks cyan, yellow or magenta, and where all three overlap it looks nearly white.
design-006.caption: Three lamps shine on one wall: red, green and blue. Find the place where the red pool and the green pool overlap. The wall there looks yellow, and in the middle, where all three overlap, it looks nearly white. Each lamp adds its light to the wall, so the overlaps are brighter than the single colors. A screen makes its yellow this way, from red light and green light together.

design-006.title: Three colored sheets over a white screen
design-006.alt: A laptop showing a plain white screen. A hand holds a yellow transparent sheet against it, overlapping a cyan sheet and a magenta sheet. Where two sheets overlap the color is darker, and where all three overlap it is very dark.
design-006.caption: Now the opposite process. The screen behind is plain white, and each transparent sheet takes some of that light away. Where the yellow sheet crosses the cyan sheet, the light that gets through both looks green. Where all three sheets cross, very little gets through and the patch is very dark. Paint and ink work on this side. Every pigment you add removes more light, so a mixture gets darker, never brighter.

design-010.title: One correction moves the whole picture
design-010.alt: Two versions of one photograph of a white lily with dark red spots, side by side. In the left version the petals look cool white and the dark background is blue-green. In the right version the petals look slightly creamy, the leaves are a yellower green and the dark background is brown.
design-010.caption: Two versions of one photograph. On the left it is as the camera recorded it, and everything leans blue: the petals, the leaves and the dark background. For the version on the right, the photographer photographed a gray surface in the same light, found the adjustment that made that gray come out gray, and applied the same adjustment here. Look at what moved: the whole picture, not only the flower. That is what a white balance correction does, and it is why this lesson has you choose which light your neutral sample stands for first.

design-013.title: The lines that letters hang on
design-013.alt: The word Sphinx in large type on a red baseline. Thin gray lines mark the ascender height, the cap height, the mean line and the descender height, and a small arrow at the right marks the x-height.
design-013.caption: The word Sphinx sits on the red baseline. Find the h. Its tall stroke rises above the small letters n and x, and that part is the ascender. Find the p. Its tail drops below the baseline, and that part is the descender. The height that n and x share is the x-height, marked by the small arrow on the right. This diagram names heights. The spaces inside letters, the counter and the aperture, are named in the diagram above.

credit.author: Max Naylor
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

design-014.title: Two typefaces, two lowercase heights
design-014.alt: The word Haxey set twice on one orange baseline. The first is in a light typeface labeled Cochin, display use and headings. The second is in heavy narrow letters labeled Impact, display and headings.
design-014.caption: Compare the lowercase letters a, x and e in these two typefaces. In Cochin, on the left, they are small beside the capital H. In Impact they come most of the way up the H. That lowercase height is called the x-height, and each typeface has its own. It is why two typefaces can share one size setting and still look like different sizes, as the booklet in this lesson did.

credit.author: Blythwood
credit.changes: Cropped, resized and converted to WebP.

design-016.title: Two narrow columns, printed in the 1450s
design-016.alt: A page from an early printed Bible. Dense black text is set in two narrow columns side by side, with one red initial and a heading in red and blue letters, on a pale, worn page.
design-016.caption: Look at how this page is set: two narrow columns side by side, not one wide block. Each line holds only a few words, so the eye has a short trip back to the start of the next one. This is a page of the Bible that Johannes Gutenberg printed in Mainz in the 1450s, with 42 lines to a column. Whatever the printer's reasons were, the effect is the one this lesson tests: a short line gives the eye an easy return.

credit.author: Johannes Gutenberg (printer)
credit.changes: Cropped, resized and converted to WebP.

design-017.title: The letter and its block are separate sizes
design-017.alt: Four gray blocks of metal type side by side, numbered 1 to 4, each with a raised white letter H on its front. Blocks 1 and 4 carry a large H and blocks 2 and 3 a smaller H. Blocks 1 and 3 are taller than blocks 2 and 4.
design-017.caption: These are four pieces of metal type, each a block with a raised H on it. Compare blocks 2 and 3. They carry the same small H, but block 3 is cast on a taller block. Lines set from block 3 would sit farther apart, although no letter grew. Blocks 1 and 4 show the reverse: the same large H, with a shorter block under number 4. In metal type the block set the distance between lines, and the letter was a separate size. That is the split this lesson asks you to keep.

credit.author: Любослов Езыкин
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

design-018.title: Kerning moves one pair
design-018.alt: The letter pairs AV and Wa set twice. In the upper row, labeled No kerning, one thin blue line separates the two letters of each pair. In the lower row, labeled Kerning applied, the letters sit closer together and two blue lines show their boxes overlapping.
design-018.caption: Compare the two rows. In the upper row each letter keeps to its own box, and the slanted sides of the A and the V leave a wide wedge of white between them. In the lower row the second letter of each pair has moved left until its box overlaps the first, and the wedge has closed. Nothing else about the letters changed. That local move is kerning. Tracking would have changed every gap in a word by the same amount.

credit.author: Sherbyte
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

design-018.title: When two letters get too close
design-018.alt: Three numbered rows of large letters. Row 1 reads morn. Row 2 shows the word twice: first with its r and n in gray, pushed close together, then in black with the two letters touching. Row 3 reads mom.
design-018.caption: A memory hook. Row 1 is the word morn. In row 2 its r and n are pushed together, first in gray and then in black, until they touch. Row 3 is the word mom. The last line of row 2 is hard to tell from row 3, because a touching r and n make the shape of an m. A gap that is too wide is not the only way a letter pair can fail.
design-018.punchline: Kern too tight and morn turns into mom

design-021.title: A sign ranked for someone in a hurry
design-021.alt: A blue airport sign hanging from a ceiling. Each line starts with an arrow and a small symbol. It reads Gates 25-40 with an arrow pointing left and Gates 7-16 with an arrow pointing up. Below, on a gray band, it reads Multi faith area with an arrow pointing left. The gate numbers are set larger than the word Gates.
design-021.caption: Read this sign the way a hurrying passenger would. The arrows come first, at the left edge. Then compare the type sizes: the gate numbers are larger and heavier than the word Gates in front of them. The number is the thing a passenger is hunting for, so it gets the most weight, and the word everyone expects gets less. Your ticket needs the same ranking, with Gate C in the place of these numbers. The sign hangs in a London airport.

design-026.title: A cue placed where the hand goes
design-026.alt: Two wooden door edges meeting in the middle of the picture. Each carries a dark square plate with two words in pale letters: Bruigh, with an accent on the u, and Push.
design-026.caption: Each of these doors carries a plate with one instruction on it, written twice: Brúigh, which is Irish, and Push. The cue sits on the door itself, at the place where you would act, and it names the action. Nobody has to try the door to find out what it does. Your gallery card needs the same thing for each of its two actions: a visible cue, at the control, that says what will happen. These doors are at a visitor centre on the Dingle Peninsula in Ireland.

credit.work: Signs-1160236, Dingle Peninsula, Co. Kerry, Ireland
credit.author: Mucklagh

design-031.title: A signal that does not rely on color
design-031.alt: A horizontal traffic signal on a pole in front of trees. Its lights have different shapes: a red square on the left, which is lit, a diamond in the middle and a third light on the right.
design-031.caption: Look at the shapes of the lights. The red one, which is lit, is a square, and the one beside it is a diamond. This signal was designed in Canada for drivers who cannot tell the colors apart. Each color has its own shape, so the lit square says stop even to someone who cannot see that it is red. The shape is a second channel for the same meaning. On your map the second channel is words, and the test is the same: take the color away and check that the status survives.

design-037.title: Direction before detail
design-037.alt: A quick red chalk sketch on brown paper. A woman on the left bends far forward and points with one outstretched arm. A small child in a padded hat stands in the middle, held by a second woman who stoops on the right.
design-037.caption: Rembrandt drew this in red chalk around 1635: two women helping a small child to walk. Look at the woman on the left. Her bent back is one long curve, and her pointing arm carries it on in a straight line. There are almost no details. The faces are a few marks and the hands are barely there. Yet you can tell who is leaning, who is steadying, and where the weight is. The directions were set down first, and they carry the drawing.

credit.work: Two women teaching a child to walk (red chalk, about 1635 to 1637)
credit.author: Rembrandt

design-039.title: One edge, two shapes
design-039.alt: A pale vase shape on a black background. The black areas on each side of it have the outline of a human face in profile, so that two faces look at each other across the vase.
design-039.caption: Look at the pale shape and you see a vase. Look at the black areas and you see two faces in profile, nose to nose. Nothing moved. The edge of the vase is the edge of each face. The space between two things is a shape with real edges, and those edges belong to the things as well. That is why the wedge between your spoon and your spatula can tell you which of their angles is wrong.

credit.author: Nevit Dilmen
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

design-040.title: A drawing course that starts with the envelope
design-040.alt: A pale printed plate headed Le Cardinal Ximenes, showing the same head in profile three times. On the left it is a few straight lines with short cross marks. In the middle the outline is made of shorter straight lines. On the right it is a finished, shaded profile of a bearded man.
design-040.caption: Read this plate from left to right. It comes from a drawing course published in Paris in the late 1860s. On the left the head is only a few straight lines: its overall height, the slope of the face, and short marks where the features will fall. In the middle those lines are broken into shorter ones. Curves, hair and shading appear only on the right. Every later stage sits inside the first envelope. Your shoe starts the same way.

credit.work: Drawing Course (Cours de dessin), plate 32, Le Cardinal Ximenes
credit.author: Charles Bargue
credit.changes: Contrast raised and converted to WebP.

design-041.title: Parallel rails meeting at one point
design-041.alt: A straight railway track seen from between the rails. The two rails and the gravel bed narrow into the distance and meet at a single point on a flat horizon, under a pale sky.
design-041.caption: Follow the two rails away from you. They stay the same distance apart all the way along, yet in the picture they close in on each other and meet at one point on the horizon. The edges of the gravel bed run the same way as the rails, and they head for that same point. A drawn box works like this. Each family of parallel edges gets one meeting point, and the points all sit on one eye level.

design-041.title: A painted square built on one point
design-041.alt: A wide fresco. A row of robed figures stands across the front of a large paved square. Pale lines in the paving run back toward a domed building in the middle, with an arch on each side and small figures in the distance.
design-041.caption: Look at the pale lines in the paving. The ones that run away from you all aim at one point, at the doorway of the building in the middle. Pietro Perugino painted this fresco in the Sistine Chapel in 1481 and 1482. The large figures in front, the small ones far back and the paving all agree with that one point, and that agreement is what makes the square look deep.

credit.work: Delivery of the Keys (Consegna delle chiavi)
credit.author: Pietro Perugino

design-042.title: One cloth sorted into light and dark
design-042.alt: A gray monochrome study of heavy cloth draped over the knees of a seated figure. Broad folds catch pale light on top and fall into deep dark hollows between them.
design-042.caption: This study of cloth over a seated figure is attributed to Leonardo da Vinci and was made around 1470. Squint at it. It shows one piece of cloth, a single material, yet some parts are painted almost white and others nearly black. The folds look solid because the patches fall into a few clear groups, light, middle and dark, and each patch sits in the group its light earned. That is the sorting this lesson asks for before any texture.

credit.work: Drapery Study for a Seated Figure
credit.author: Attributed to Leonardo da Vinci

design-043.title: Three kinds of edge in one painting
design-043.alt: A painting of a girl looking over her shoulder against a dark background. She wears a blue and yellow headscarf, a pearl earring, a white collar and a yellow-brown jacket. Light falls on her face from the left.
design-043.caption: Vermeer painted this around 1665. Find three kinds of edge. The white collar stops sharply against the jacket, like the cliff in this lesson. On her cheek the light fades into shade with no line at all, like the beach. Then look below the hanging end of the scarf, on the right. The shaded jacket and the dark background are so close in value that the boundary between them disappears. Each edge was chosen from the values on either side of it.

credit.work: Girl with a Pearl Earring (Meisje met de parel)
credit.author: Johannes Vermeer

design-044.title: Two shadows with two causes
design-044.alt: A computer-drawn pale gray ball on a white ground, lit from the upper right. The lower left side of the ball is in shade, and a dark oval shadow with a sharp edge lies on the ground to its left.
design-044.caption: This ball was drawn by a computer with one small light at the upper right, so no second lamp muddles it. Find the two dark areas. The dim side of the ball is the form shadow: that surface faces away from the light, and nothing is in its way. The dark oval on the ground is the cast shadow: the ground there would be lit if the ball were not blocking it. Run this lesson's check. The cast shadow lies on the side away from the light. Its edge is unusually sharp because the light here is a single point.

design-047.title: Three materials under one light
design-047.alt: A still life painting of a table with a dark green cloth. On it are gray metal plates holding oysters and a half-peeled lemon, a tall green-stemmed glass of wine, an overturned glass, and an ornate silver dish on a stem lying on its side.
design-047.caption: Three kinds of surface share one light on this table: dull gray metal plates, a clear glass and a polished silver dish lying on its side. Willem Claesz. Heda painted them in 1635. Compare how the light ends on each. On the plates it spreads into broad, soft grays. On the glass and the silver it shrinks to small, hard-edged spots. No single mark means shiny. Each material is told by the size of its light patches and by how sharply they stop.

fg-002.title: Each group rises, the total falls
fg-002.alt: A chart with four blue points rising along a blue line at the upper left and four red points rising along a red line at the lower right. A dashed black line fitted to all eight points slopes downward.
fg-002.caption: A different drawing of the same trap. The four blue points rise from left to right, and so do the four red points. Now fit one line to all eight together. It is the dashed line, and it falls. Each group says up and the pooled data says down. Neither reading is a mistake. The two groups sit in different places, and the pooled line mostly measures the gap between them. At your repair desk the mixture of jobs plays the part of that gap.

credit.author: Schutz
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

fg-013.title: Blades bent by the camera
fg-013.alt: An aircraft propeller seen from a cabin window against blue sky, with the ground far below. Its dark blades appear as long curved hooks of different shapes in front of a gray engine housing.
fg-013.caption: A phone took this through an aircraft window. The blades look like long curved hooks, and no two of them have the same shape. The strong curves were made by the camera. It recorded the picture row by row, each row a moment after the one before, and the blades kept turning. Every row caught each blade at a slightly different angle, and the stacked rows drew a curve. Notice that the blades are bent but not smeared. Bending comes from the timing of the rows. Smearing comes from how long each row gathers light.

fg-014.title: Bands the wall does not have
fg-014.alt: A small photograph of a red brick wall with a concrete pillar on the left, a bare tree at its foot and one curved shadow. Several slanted bands of lighter and darker tone cross the brickwork to the right of the shadow.
fg-014.caption: Look at the brickwork to the right of the curved shadow. Slanted bands cross it from the lower left to the upper right. The wall has no such bands. This is a photograph of a brick wall that was reduced to a very small size, and the fine, regular rows of bricks could not survive the reduction. A false pattern, far coarser than any brick, took their place. The curved dark shape on the left is a real shadow. The next picture shows the same wall larger.

fg-014.title: The same wall with enough detail
fg-014.alt: The same red brick wall at a larger size, with the concrete pillar on the left, the bare tree and the one curved shadow. The rows of bricks are distinct and no slanted bands cross them.
fg-014.caption: This is the same photograph at a larger size. Each row of bricks is distinct, and the slanted bands are gone. The curved shadow is still there, because it was really on the wall. That is the test this lesson gives you: a pattern that appears or disappears when only the size of the picture changes was made by the sampling. If you see faint bands here as well, your own screen added them while fitting the picture, which is why the lesson has you record the viewing stage.

fg-015.title: Equal time, unequal gaps
fg-015.alt: A single photograph on a black background showing a yellow basketball many times over, along two arcs of a bounce. The images of the ball are crowded together at the top of each arc and spread far apart near the floor.
fg-015.caption: A flash fired 25 times a second while this ball bounced, so each image of the ball comes the same slice of time after the last. Now read the gaps. Near the top of each arc the images crowd together, because the ball was moving slowly there. Near the floor they are far apart, because it was moving fast. The time step never changed and the spacing did. Your paper counter slows down the same way: one picture per position, with the positions drawn closer together.

fg-016.title: A caption for a sound, not a line
fg-016.alt: A black and white film frame of two men in suits standing in a sitting room, one wearing a bowler hat. A caption across the lower part of the picture reads KNOCKING ON DOOR in square brackets.
fg-016.caption: The picture alone does not explain what these two men will do next. The caption does: someone is knocking at the door. The square brackets mark the words as a sound and not as a line of speech. A viewer who cannot hear the soundtrack gets the same information as one who can, at the moment it matters. The frame is from Unaccustomed As We Are, a Laurel and Hardy film from 1929.

credit.work: Unaccustomed As We Are (1929 film), frame with a closed caption
credit.author: Lewis R. Foster

fg-017.title: A circle laid flat, by ruler
fg-017.alt: An old printed diagram marked F.6. At the bottom a circle is drawn inside a square that is ruled into small squares. Above it the same ruled square is drawn receding into the distance, as a shape that narrows toward the top, and the circle inside it has become a flattened oval.
fg-017.caption: This diagram comes from a printed edition of Leon Battista Alberti's treatise on painting, which he wrote in the 1430s. At the bottom is a circle in a ruled square, seen face-on. Above it the same square lies flat and recedes, and the circle has flattened into an oval. Compare the two with this lesson's two spans: how wide, and how open. The opening from top to bottom is what has collapsed. The diagram finds the oval with ruled lines. This lesson asks you to find it by looking at the lid.

credit.work: Della pittura, diagram of a circle in perspective
credit.author: Leon Battista Alberti

fg-018.title: Every gray here is made of black lines
fg-018.alt: A greatly enlarged detail of an old engraving. Pale folds of cloth surround a flat shaded surface that carries a few small angular shapes. Every tone is built from fine parallel black lines, and in the darker areas a second set of lines crosses the first.
fg-018.caption: This is a small detail of an engraving by Albrecht Dürer, greatly enlarged. No gray ink was used. Every tone is made of black lines on white paper. Find a light fold: the lines there are thin and widely spaced. Find a dark hollow: a second set of lines crosses the first, and the white gaps shrink to specks. Notice also that the lines bend with the cloth. Their spacing sets the tone, and their direction describes the surface.

credit.work: Detail of an engraving, showing hatching
credit.author: Albrecht Dürer

fg-019.title: Low light draws every ripple
fg-019.alt: A close view of wet sand covered in small ripples that run in two directions, with a small coiled worm cast near the top. Each ripple is bright on one side and dark on the other.
fg-019.caption: Nobody outlined these ripples. The photographer notes that the light was low evening light, and that light is doing the describing: each ridge is bright on one side and dark beyond it. Find one dark shape and point to the ridge that stands between it and the light. Then imagine the sun overhead. The same sand would look almost flat. Some of the dark here is a ridge turning away from the light, which this lesson calls form shading. For your study, keep only the patches whose blocking ridge you can point to.

fg-020.title: A drawing ruled into squares
fg-020.alt: An old pen drawing of a monument: a rider on a horse on top of a tall pedestal, with figures seated and standing around its base. Faint ruled lines divide the whole sheet into squares.
fg-020.caption: Look for the faint ruled lines that divide this whole sheet into squares. The drawing is a design for a monument, made around 1735. A grid like this was the usual way to copy a drawing at another size. The same number of squares is ruled on the new surface, larger or smaller, and the drawing is carried across one square at a time. Inside each square there is only a little to place. Your leaf goes from 4 centimeters to 8 by the same method.

credit.work: Design for a Monument to Emperor Charles VI of Naples (about 1735)
credit.author: Unknown artist

life-001.title: Same size, different type
life-001.alt: A hand holds a flat, pale mesh filter panel at an angle in front of a dark furnace cabinet that carries yellow warning labels.
life-001.caption: The photographer describes this as a washable, reusable filter measuring 16 by 25 inches. Compare that with the purchase note in this lesson: nominal sixteen by twenty-five by one inch, disposable pleated. The two numbers given match. The type does not, and neither a thickness nor a rating is given. On this lesson's checklist that is a match on two numbers, a change of type and two unknowns, so it is a question for the property manager and not a purchase. A match on the size printed on the front is where the check starts, not where it ends.

life-003.title: A felt of lint on the screen
life-003.alt: A hand holds a hinged plastic lint screen, opened flat, in front of the round opening of a dryer. Both mesh halves are coated with gray lint, thickest on the upper half.
life-003.caption: This is the felt of fluff from the start of this lesson. The mesh of this screen is almost completely covered, so the warm, damp air leaving the drum has to push through the lint as well as the mesh. Less air gets through, and the machine runs hotter. Clearing a screen like this is the one job the lesson leaves to you. This one opens like a book. Yours may look different, so follow the instructions for your own model.

life-004.title: Water that came out of the air
life-004.alt: A hand in a dark sleeve reaches up to a fogged window pane. A finger has written the word ALASKA in the mist and underlined it. Drops of water run down the glass.
life-004.caption: The mist on this glass is condensation: water that left the air when the air met a cold pane, the same thing that happens to your bathroom window. Look at the letters. The finger moved the water aside, and the glass is clear where it passed. That is all wiping does. It moves liquid that has already formed. Unless the damp air itself is taken away, the mist comes back.

life-009.title: The light comes on with range to spare
life-009.alt: A car dashboard display. It reads 71 degrees Fahrenheit, then RANGE 24 miles. A fuel bar running from E to F is lit only at the E end. Below the display an orange fuel pump warning light is on.
life-009.caption: The orange pump at the bottom is the fuel light from this lesson. Now read the line above it: range 24 miles. The light is on, and the car can still drive to a petrol station. It did not wait for zero. That margin is the whole design, and your reorder signal needs the same property: it has to fire while the stock on the shelf still covers the wait for more.

life-024.title: A measured draw, not a label
life-024.alt: A gray plug-in energy monitor in a British wall socket, with an appliance's white plug pushed into its front. Its small screen shows the number 10 above a row of buttons.
life-024.caption: This monitor sits between the wall socket and the plug, and its screen shows what the appliance is drawing at this moment. The photographer records the reading as 10 watts. That is a measured figure for actual use, the kind this lesson asks for, and it can sit far below the maximum printed on a label. It is still a rate, like a speedometer reading. Multiply it by your hours, divide by 1,000 and multiply by your tariff before you call it a cost.

credit.work: Plug-in power and energy monitor in a UK mains socket
credit.author: Gareth.randall

life-026.title: Brand on top, identity underneath
life-026.alt: A metal nameplate fixed with two screws to a green machine. The top line reads Malmbergs in large letters. Below it: Three-phase induction motor, Frame MS 711-2, and a grid of ratings such as kW 0.37, RPM 2730 and V 230/400. The last entry reads NO. 1212073091.
life-026.caption: Read this plate from the top. The largest word is the brand. It tells you who made the motor, and it would look the same on every motor from that maker. The identity is in the small print underneath: the frame designation, MS 711-2, and the ratings beside it. Those are the characters to compare, one by one, with what a manual says it covers. The entry at the bottom right, marked NO., is most likely a serial number. That one names a single motor, and it is the part to keep out of public searches.

life-030.title: The line, printed on the device
life-030.alt: The printed label on the back of a black battery charger. Under the model and the input and output figures, a warning reads: Do not remove cover or back plate. No user-serviceable parts inside. Refer service to qualified service agent. A boxed caution below adds: Do not disassemble unit.
life-030.caption: Read the warning in the middle of this label: do not remove cover, no user-serviceable parts inside, refer service to qualified service agent. That is the line between owner and technician from this lesson, and here the maker has printed it on the product. Notice what the label does not mention: screws. It does not say the case is hard to open. It says who should open it. This is a charger, not the speaker in the example, and the rule has the same form.

credit.author: Raimond Spekking
credit.changes: Cropped, resized and converted to WebP.

life-031.title: A thermometer, and where the raw chicken sits
life-031.alt: A hand holds a dial marked Refrigerator Freezer Thermometer inside a refrigerator. Its needle points to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. On the shelf behind it are a bowl of fruit, a box of fried chicken and a dish of chopped tomato. A tray of raw chicken sits on the shelf below.
life-031.caption: Two things from this lesson are in one photograph from the United States Department of Agriculture. The first is the dial in the hand. It is a thermometer, not a control, and its needle sits close to 40 degrees Fahrenheit, about 4 degrees Celsius, which is the upper limit in the guidance. The second is at the bottom of the picture. The raw chicken is on the shelf below the fruit and the cooked food, so nothing can drip from it onto food that is eaten as it is.

credit.work: Food Safety - Cut Waste in Refrigerators (20120106-OC-AMW-0073)
credit.author: U.S. Department of Agriculture

life-038.title: The contacts on a spare battery
life-038.alt: A black rechargeable camera battery lying on a dark surface. Its label reads Battery Pack, 7.2V, Rechargeable Li-ion, 1920mAh 14Wh. Small metal contacts sit in recesses at the left end.
life-038.caption: This is a spare lithium battery for a camera. Look at its left end. The small metal contacts in the recesses are the terminals of this lesson, and loose in a pocket they are what a key or a coin could bridge. The label also states the size of the battery, 14 Wh, which is the kind of figure that limits on size are written in. A spare like this passes the location rule only in the cabin, and the container rule only with those contacts covered. Check the current guidance for your own flight.

life-039.title: The frame tests the packed bag
life-039.alt: A white baggage sizer on an airport floor: an open frame with a tray at the bottom and a back panel ruled as a grid. Above it stands a tall blue board headed Carry-On Baggage Allowance. A red queue ribbon and check-in desks are behind.
life-039.caption: This is the frame from this lesson, at an airport check-in. Look at its shape: a fixed opening with a ruled grid behind it. A bag passes only if all of it goes in, wheels, handle and bulging front pocket included. The frame cannot read a label that says cabin size, and it gives no credit for fitting on two sides out of three. This one stands at Taichung Airport in Taiwan. Your own flight has its own numbers, and they are on your booking.

credit.work: Korean Air baggage sizer, Taichung Airport
credit.author: Saimmx

mind-007.title: Try the puzzle both ways
mind-007.alt: Two nearly identical cartoon pictures side by side. Each shows an old woman with glasses and a red-haired child behind a large pink layered cake, a white cat at the right, a wall clock, a cooking pot on a shelf, bananas, cherries and a tray of baking. Small details differ between the two pictures.
mind-007.caption: A real spot-the-difference puzzle. First try it the hard way: look at the left picture only, cover it, then look at the right one and say what changed. Then look at both together and go item to item, clock to clock, shelf to shelf, tray to tray. The differences that hid from your memory show up when both versions are in view. That is all this lesson asks you to do with the two invitations.

mind-028.title: A sketch of forgetting and reviewing
mind-028.alt: A chart titled The Forgetting Curve, with Memory on the vertical axis and days 1 to 6 on the horizontal axis. A red curve falls steeply from the top left. Green curves start again from the top at day 1, day 2 and day 3, and each one falls more slowly than the one before.
mind-028.caption: The red curve is memory after a single study session: a steep drop, then a long slow tail. Each green curve starts at a later review. It begins at the top again and falls more slowly than the curve before it. That is the idea behind spacing: a later encounter restores the memory and also makes the next gap safer. Read this as a sketch, not as a measurement. The curves are smooth because they were drawn that way, and no chart can tell you the right number of days for your own words.

credit.author: Icez
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

money-006.title: Find the assumptions on this curve
money-006.alt: A chart titled Compound Interest, with the subtitle 15% compounding annual interest on the principal. A green area starts at a 10,000 dollar initial investment, stays low for about the first twenty years and then climbs steeply to more than 2.5 million dollars at year 40.
money-006.caption: A smooth, persuasive curve, so do what this lesson says and find its assumptions. They sit in small print: 15% a year, on a single 10,000 dollars, for 40 years. Rebuild the first two points by hand. 10,000 times 1.15 is 11,500, and 11,500 times 1.15 is 13,225. The curve is that same multiplication done 40 times. The steep end is correct arithmetic. The part to question is the 15%, because the chart does not say where a steady 15% a year would come from.

money-009.title: Fifty thousand million marks
money-009.alt: A German banknote printed in black on cream paper with a blue-green tint in the middle. Large orange figures of 50 stand in the corners. The lettering reads Reichsbanknote, Fünfzig Milliarden Mark, and the small print gives the place and date Berlin, 10 October 1923.
money-009.caption: A memory hook. This German banknote is dated 10 October 1923, during the hyperinflation of that year. Its face value is fünfzig Milliarden Mark: fifty thousand million marks. A person holding it had a larger number than anyone in this lesson and a very poor ruler, because the same note bought less and less as the weeks went by. The number on the paper is the coin count. The question that matters is how many baskets it buys at today's prices.
money-009.punchline: Count in loaves, not in coins.

money-031.title: A message that brings its own checker
money-031.alt: A made-up email under a TrustedBank logo. It tells a valued customer that a withdrawal of $135.25 was attempted from their account in another country, and asks them to visit the website through the link below to verify their personal information. A blue underlined web address follows, and the email is signed TrustedBank.
money-031.caption: This email was made up as an example, and the bank does not exist. Read it for its shape. It announces a problem: a withdrawal abroad that may not have been yours. Then it supplies the helper: the link below. Ask this lesson's question of that link: who gave me this? The message did. So the link is the card from the man at the door, however official the logo looks. The spelling slips, recieved and discrepency, are a bonus. A message with perfect spelling gets the same question.

credit.work: Example of a phishing email from a fictional bank
credit.author: Andrew Levine

money-034.title: Underline the claims, circle the request
money-034.alt: A mock-up of a scam page. A white box headed This page says warns in capital letters that the device is infected with many trojans and tells the reader to call certified technicians on a blanked-out number. Behind it a blue screen titled Critical Windows Error repeats the warning, says do not restart and gives the same blanked-out toll free number.
money-034.caption: This is a demonstration, not a real pop-up, and its maker says the claims in it are deliberately unrealistic. Do this lesson's exercise on it. Underline what is claimed: many trojans, 11 viruses, a firewall at 5 percent. Circle what is requested: call this number immediately. Then read the first three words of the white box: This page says. A page can draw a blue error screen as easily as it draws an advert. Close it with the browser's own controls.

credit.work: Example of a technical support scam popup
credit.author: Pahunkat

money-036.title: Equal payments, shrinking interest
money-036.alt: A wide bar chart with amounts in pounds on its vertical axis and dates from 2013 to 2018 along the bottom. Every bar has the same height. In each bar a gray part at the bottom, named Interest in the key, gets smaller from left to right while the green part above it, named Principal, gets larger, until the last bars are almost entirely green.
money-036.caption: Each bar is one payment, and all the bars are the same height, like the 50-unit bucket. Inside a bar, the gray part at the bottom is that period's interest and the green part is principal. Follow the gray from left to right. It shrinks with every payment, because each payment lowers the debt that the next interest charge is worked out on. That is the pattern of month one and month two in this lesson, continued to the end of a loan. The source describes it from the side of an investor who lends the money and receives the same two parts.

observer-001.title: Two words that label a guess
observer-001.alt: The upper part of a handwritten notebook page in ink. The words I think stand alone at the top left. Below them is a small branching sketch like a tree, with the number 1 in a circle at its root and the letters A, B, C and D at the ends of branches. More handwriting runs down the right side.
observer-001.caption: This is part of a page from a notebook that Charles Darwin kept in 1837. Read the two words at the top before you look at the sketch: I think. The branching drawing under them is an idea about how species might be related. It is not a thing he saw. Whatever he meant by them, those two words do the job of this lesson's second column. A reader can tell at once that what follows is a possible explanation and not an observation, which is what lets a later reader correct it.

credit.work: Tree sketch in a notebook on the transmutation of species (1837)
credit.author: Charles Darwin
credit.changes: Cropped, resized and converted to WebP.

observer-004.title: A seat with a view of a bush
observer-004.alt: A wooden bench, seen from behind, stands on a paved patch of ground and faces a tall, leafy bush that rises directly in front of it. Water and a car park are visible in the distance, but only to the left of the bush. The sky is blue with white clouds.
observer-004.caption: A memory hook. Draw the sightline from this bench to the water. It runs straight into the bush. Whoever sits here can report the bush in fine detail and cannot report a boat passing behind it, however carefully they look. That is the restricted-view seat of this lesson, outdoors. When two accounts differ, check the seat before you judge the person who sat in it.
observer-004.punchline: Being there is not the same as being able to see it.

tech-006.title: The four messages, top to bottom
tech-006.alt: A diagram with two vertical lines labeled client and server and an arrow labeled time pointing down. Four arrows cross between the lines, from top to bottom: Discover from client to server, Offer from server to client, Request from client to server and Acknowledge from server to client.
tech-006.caption: Read the arrows from top to bottom, because time runs down the page. Discover and Request leave the client. Offer and Acknowledge, which this lesson calls ACK, come back from the server. Now cover the bottom arrow with a finger. What remains is the capture from this lesson: the printer asked, a server proposed and the printer chose, and nothing confirms the lease. The diagram leaves the relay out. A relay only carries these same four messages between the two sides.

credit.author: Gelmo96
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

tech-008.title: The chain a resolver walks for you
tech-008.alt: A diagram. A box labeled DNS Iterator asks: Where's www.wikipedia.org? Three numbered exchanges follow. A root nameserver replies with the address of another server to try. The org nameserver replies with a third address to try. The wikipedia.org nameserver replies: It's at, followed by a row of x's in place of the address.
tech-008.caption: The box on the left is a resolver with no stored answer, so it has to ask. Follow the numbers. First it asks a root server, which does not hold the answer and names a server to try next. That one, the server for names ending in org, names a third. The third is the authority for wikipedia.org, and it gives the address. Your device makes none of these trips. It asks its resolver once and waits, as you would wait at the receptionist's desk. The drawing hides the final address behind a row of x's. The order of the questions is the point.

credit.work: Example of an iterative DNS resolver
credit.author: Lion Kimbro
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

tech-011.title: The trip has a length you can see
tech-011.alt: An old printed world map titled Eastern Telegraph Co's System and its General Connections. Red lines mark undersea telegraph cables. A thick bundle of them crosses the North Atlantic between Britain and North America. Others run down the coasts of Africa and South America and on to India, East Asia, Australia and New Zealand.
tech-011.caption: This chart from about 1901 marks the telegraph cables of its time in red. Each red line across an ocean is a real length of cable lying on the sea floor, and a message had to travel all of it. That part has not changed. A request from your editor still crosses real distance, there and back, and that travel sits inside the 60 milliseconds of this lesson's budget. A faster plan widens the pipe at your end of the cable. It does not bring the two ends any closer together.

credit.work: Eastern Telegraph Co's System and its General Connections (chart, about 1901)
credit.author: Unknown author

tech-014.title: A limit posted before the bridge
tech-014.alt: A round road sign with a red rim stands on a post beside a stone bridge wall. Between two black triangles it reads 4.4 m and 14 feet 9 inches. A plate on the wall says whom to telephone if a vehicle strikes this railway bridge.
tech-014.caption: This sign gives the limit of the bridge twice, 4.4 metres and 14 feet 9 inches, where a driver can read it before driving under. A network link has a limit like this, called its MTU. The difference is that a packet cannot read a sign in advance. The sender learns the limit only when a router sends word back, in the note this lesson calls Packet Too Big. The plate on the wall says whom to call when a vehicle strikes the bridge anyway.

tech-014.title: A load taller than the limit
tech-014.alt: A white box lorry stopped under a steel railway bridge beside a stone wall. The roof and upper side of its box are peeled back and hang crumpled over the side. A small yellow warning sign hangs on the bridge.
tech-014.caption: This lorry was taller than the gap under the railway bridge. Its roof is peeled back, and the photographer notes that the bridge was undamaged. That is the rule in this lesson: the limit belongs to the link, and a load over the limit does not get through. A network is gentler. An IPv6 router discards the packet that is too big and sends back a note naming the limit, so that the next packet can be made to fit. The trouble in this lesson starts when that note never arrives.

thinking-004.title: Dots on the aircraft that came back
thinking-004.alt: An outline of a twin-engine aircraft seen from above, covered with red dots. The dots cluster on the outer wings, the middle of the body and the tail. The engines, the cockpit and the nose have almost none.
thinking-004.caption: This drawing is an illustration, not a record. It shows the kind of damage pattern that bombers returning from missions in the Second World War might carry, and it goes with reasoning credited to the statistician Abraham Wald in 1943. The engines and the cockpit are almost clean, and it is tempting to conclude that they were rarely hit. But this collection has a door. Only aircraft that got home could be examined. On Wald's reading, a hit to an engine was far more likely to bring an aircraft down, so that damage seldom came home to be counted. The clean areas are the hole in the table.

credit.author: Martin Grandjean (vector), McGeddon (picture), US Air Force (hit plot concept)
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

thinking-015.title: A long tail pulls the mean away
thinking-015.alt: A chart of two curves with a legend: mode in red, median in green, mean in blue. A tall, narrow solid curve has its three vertical lines close together near 1.0. A low dotted curve with a long tail to the right has its three dotted lines far apart: the red near 0.4, the green at 1.0 and the blue near 1.65.
thinking-015.caption: Start with the low dotted curve, the one with a long tail to the right. Its green line is the median: half of the values lie on each side of it. Its blue line is the mean, and the tail has dragged it out to about 1.65, well past the middle. Now look at the tall narrow curve, which has almost no tail. Its three lines nearly touch. So a wide gap between median and mean is the mark of a tail. The gallery, with a median of 0.2 seconds and a mean of 0.98, has the same mark.

credit.work: Comparison of mean, median and mode
credit.author: Cmglee
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

thinking-018.title: Every ball had the same odds
thinking-018.alt: A lit triangular board against black. Pegs fill its top corner and narrow channels run down to its base. Green balls lie piled in the channels, highest in the middle channel and lower toward both sides. A bell-shaped curve is drawn over the piles.
thinking-018.caption: This is a Galton board. Balls dropped in at the top bounce left or right off each peg and collect in the channels at the base. The drawn curve predicts where the piles will be tallest, and it is a very good prediction: the middle. Now look at single balls. Some of them sit well out to the sides, and a few lie at the far ends. Knowing the centre of this pattern as well as it can be known has not pulled one ball in from the edge. That is the second unknown in this lesson, the variation that more data cannot remove.

thinking-020.title: Tight, and off target
thinking-020.alt: A red and white target. Four black dots sit close together at the lower left, across the middle rings, well away from the centre.
thinking-020.caption: Four shots that almost touch each other, and every one of them is well away from the centre. This is the parcel scale in this lesson: its readings agree with each other, and they share one error. Imagine seeing only the four dots, with the rings hidden. You would trust that group completely. The rings are the outside reference, and without one a tight group says nothing about where the centre is.

credit.author: DarkEvil
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

thinking-020.title: Scattered, and centred
thinking-020.alt: The same red and white target. Four black dots are spread out around the centre: one above it, one on each side and one below and to the left.
thinking-020.caption: Now the four shots are spread around the centre. No single shot is in the middle, yet their average lands near it, because their errors point in different directions and partly cancel. This is the other scale in the lesson, accurate and imprecise. More shots would help this shooter. More shots would do nothing for the first one, whose every shot carries the same offset.

credit.author: DarkEvil
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

thinking-029.title: The aircraft that gave the trap a name
thinking-029.alt: A white Concorde airliner in flight against a clear blue sky, nose raised and landing gear down. The words British Airways run along its fuselage and its tail is dark blue.
thinking-029.caption: This is Concorde, a different case from the costume. The trap in this lesson is also called the Concorde fallacy. The name comes from the way the British and French governments went on paying for the aircraft's development after it had become clear that there was no longer an economic case for it. It is a standard example of treating money already spent as a reason to spend more. Notice what this lesson adds to the usual telling: the aircraft that was built still flew. What the past produced can still matter.

thinking-038.title: The big part matters more than the big multiplier
thinking-038.alt: Three horizontal bars under the words Two independent parts, A and B. The bar labeled Original process is mostly red, for part A, with a shorter blue end, for part B. In the bar labeled Make B 5x faster the blue end is tiny and the whole bar is only a little shorter. In the bar labeled Make A 2x faster the red part is halved and the whole bar is the shortest.
thinking-038.caption: The top bar is a job made of a long red part A and a short blue part B. In the second bar B has been made five times faster. That sounds dramatic, and the whole bar is barely shorter, because B was a small share to begin with. In the third bar A is only twice as fast, and the whole job is clearly the shortest of the three.
