The multiplier on a part is not the multiplier on the job. The share that part occupies decides how much shows through, as the six minutes of encoding did in the export.

credit.author: Gorivero
credit.changes: Rendered from SVG and converted to WebP.

thinking-040.title: A spacecraft lost to a missing unit
thinking-040.alt: An artist's picture of a spacecraft above a red-brown planet. Its box-shaped body is wrapped in orange and gold foil, a long solar panel in three sections reaches down to the left, and a round dish antenna stands on top. The sky behind is black with faint stars.
thinking-040.caption: This is an artist's picture of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter, which was lost as it arrived at Mars in September 1999. The investigation found a unit mismatch. One piece of software reported the push of the thrusters in pound-force seconds, and the navigation software read the same numbers as newton seconds, which made them wrong by a factor of about 4.45. It is the megabyte and megabit mistake of this lesson with another pair of units. Writing the unit beside every quantity is aimed at exactly this kind of handover.

credit.work: Artist's rendering of the Mars Climate Orbiter
credit.author: NASA/JPL/Corby Waste

wellbeing-029.title: Pulses in their dried form
wellbeing-029.alt: Open sacks seen from above at a market stall. Most hold dried seeds in many colours: yellow split pulses, dark red beans, small green beans, brown lentil-like seeds, pale round peas and black and white speckled seeds. One sack, printed with the word rice, holds small white grains, and a sack of yellow kernels shows at the right edge.
wellbeing-029.caption: Most of these sacks at a market in Darjeeling, India, hold dried pulses: split pulses, small lentils and beans in several colours. Each of those counts among the protein foods in this lesson. Each is also the flat-pack version. Nothing in these sacks is ready for a wrap today. A dried pulse needs the cooking, and often the soaking, that its own instructions give, which is why Amina reached for the tin.

credit.work: Pulses for Sale in Market - Darjeeling - West Bengal - India (12431603075)
credit.author: Adam Jones

wellbeing-032.title: The arithmetic on a real label format
wellbeing-032.alt: A black and white Nutrition Facts label in the United States format. It reads 8 servings per container, serving size 2/3 cup (55g) and calories 230 per serving, followed by rows for fat, sodium, carbohydrate, sugars and protein beside a percent daily value column.
wellbeing-032.caption: This is the sample label that the United States food regulator published in 2016. Read the two lines above the big number first. The 230 calories belong to one serving of 55 grams, and the container holds 8 servings. Do the hotel arithmetic: 8 times 230 is 1,840 calories in the whole container. The same multiplier applies to every row, so 160 milligrams of sodium per serving is 1,280 in the pack. None of this says how much to eat. It says which quantity each number belongs to.

work-003.title: Plates in the air
work-003.alt: A man in a dark jacket and bow tie stands behind a table on a stage, looking up, with one hand on a tall thin pole. Six poles rise from the table. A plate sits on top of five of them, and a stack of plates lies on the table.
work-003.caption: Count the plates in the air: five, on five poles. Now count the plates in his hands: none. Every one of the five is still his. Each will wobble, and when it does it will need him. Look where his eyes are. Work waiting on a reviewer or a reply is a plate on a pole. The stack on the table is the dashboard request: before another plate goes up, one of the five has to finish, pause by agreement or move. The performer is Henrik Bothe.

work-026.title: A list read at the moment it decides something
work-026.alt: An aircraft cockpit in dim light with lit instrument panels. A pilot in a flight suit and headset looks down at a sheet in his lap, lit by a red light. Lights on the ground show through the windows.
work-026.caption: A pilot reads a pre-flight checklist before a refuelling mission, in a photograph from the United States Air Force. Notice when this is happening: on the ground, before take-off, at the last moment when a missed item is still easy to fix. That is the trigger. Each line on a list like this names a thing to look at and the state it should be in, and the pilot looks. Ticking the sheet in his lap proves nothing by itself. It points him at the evidence on the panel in front of him.
